This part reads customer-service calls, the daytime charge and a few states, and acts on 1292 of 4000 training customers, 185 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 1% without it and about 5% with it.

Through it, more calls raise the chance in an uneven way, for the typical customer it acts on from about 1% at 0 to about 13% at 3 calls, and a higher daytime charge lowers it in an uneven way, only while the charge stays below about 25.31 US dollars (between 23.90 and 28.72 US dollars for different customers): for a typical customer from about 9% at 19.07 to about 3% at 42.40 US dollars.
The charge counts more, in stages, for customers with more than 1 call (from about 18% to about 3%, against about 9% to about 3%) and for customers in New Hampshire (from about 24% to about 1%).

This part reads customer-service calls and the daytime charge: calls add only from about 3 calls upwards, slowly at first, then faster, in an uneven way (for a typical such customer from about 3% to about 12%), and a daytime charge above about 32.03 US dollars takes this away, mostly in a jump around that point.
This part reads daytime minutes and adds to the chance only once they rise above about 216 minutes, then steadily: for a typical customer from about 3% at 112 to about 6% at 249 minutes.
It acts on 1002 of 4000 training customers, 285 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 7% without it and about 12% with it.
Across the whole model, daytime minutes raise the chance slowly at first, then faster, from about 1% to about 21% outside New York and from about 1% to about 18% in New York.

This part acts on every customer outside Maryland (3918 of 4000 training customers, 547 of whom left) and lowers their chance, for its typical customer from about 12% to about 3%; through it, a customer in Maryland has about 12% instead of about 3%.

This part adds to the chance only once account length rises above about 147, then steadily, by less than a point; it acts on 488 of 4000 training customers, 77 of whom left (for its typical customer about 3% without it and about 4% with it).
This part reads only the state; its formula reproduces it exactly on all 4000 training customers.
This part reads the state but is switched off, so it barely changes the predictions.
